ai-at-work.title: Apple approves Poke as the first AI agent on its Messages for Business platform
ai-at-work.excerpt: Poke, the startup that lets people use AI agents through simple text messages, has become the first AI agent approved for Apple’s Messages for Business platform.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Apple just gave its blessing to Poke, an AI agent that works through text messages, making it the first of its kind on the Messages for Business platform. This matters because it signals Apple is finally opening its walled garden to practical AI tools that employees actually use every day instead of pretending AI assistants nobody wants are the future. After years of playing it safe, Apple's moving into the space where real work happens, though I'd bet half my keyboard that their approval process was more about control than innovation.

ai-at-work.title: Meta rolls out a new AI creator assistant on Facebook

ai-at-work.dwp_take: Meta launched an AI assistant that answers creator questions about posting timing and comment sentiment instead of making them dig through analytics dashboards. This matters because digital workplace teams are watching how AI simplifies data access across platforms, and many are betting their own creator and community programs on similar natural language interfaces. Honestly, if Meta can make creators stop obsessing over vanity metrics through a chatbot, that's a genuine win, though I'd need to see the actual advice quality before throwing a parade.

tools-tech.title: I have a new favorite Linux email client in 2026 - and I've tested them all
tools-tech.excerpt: A cross-platform app for Linux, MacOS and Windows, Aerion supports all the features I need, without the extra clutter.
tools-tech.dwp_take: A writer tested multiple Linux email clients and settled on Aerion as their preferred choice, citing its cross-platform compatibility and feature-complete design without unnecessary bloat. This matters to digital workplace folks because email infrastructure decisions still drive productivity, and developers choosing lightweight alternatives signals that the industry is finally rejecting feature-bloated enterprise mail clients. After three decades watching people suffer through Outlook, it's genuinely refreshing to see someone excited about email software that actually does its job without making you want to take a walk.

tools-tech.title: Why Apple may be winning again

tools-tech.dwp_take: Apple is making strategic moves around Vision Pro and other products that position them for growth in ways competitors aren't expecting. Here's the thing though: Apple announcing a product and actually getting enterprise adoption are two different sports, and I've watched enough conference keynotes to know that "immense consequences" and "counter-intuitive gambits" are corporate speak for "we'll see what sticks in twelve months."

tools-tech.title: Anthropic suggests slowing AI research until we can align it with human goals

tools-tech.dwp_take: Anthropic researchers are calling for the AI industry to pump the brakes on development until we figure out how to make AI systems actually do what we want them to do instead of going rogue. This matters because digital workplaces are already deploying AI tools for knowledge work, content creation, and decision-making, so if we're worried about alignment at the research level, we should probably be nervous about what's running in your Slack and email right now. Look, I've seen enough enterprise software implementations go sideways to know that "we'll figure out the safety part later" is how you end up explaining to executives why their new AI assistant invented a fictional product line.

tools-tech.title: Compliance chaos: NY regulators see a data breach — then focus on IT errors
tools-tech.excerpt: The age-old IT defense when compliance violations are investigated by regulators is to try and keep a low profile — and hope no one looks too closely. But with enhanced SEC interest in all data breach
tools-tech.dwp_take: New York regulators discovered a data breach and then pivoted to investigating the IT failures that enabled it, signaling a shift toward holding technical teams accountable rather than just documenting incidents. Digital workplace leaders need to understand that regulators are now examining the root causes of breaches, not just the breaches themselves, which means your IT infrastructure and compliance documentation are getting real scrutiny. After three decades watching IT teams try the "hope they don't look too hard" strategy, I can tell you that era is officially over, and frankly, good riddance.

digital-culture.title: Employees aren’t resisting AI—they’re resisting fear
digital-culture.excerpt: Across all industries, an unmistakable tension is building inside of organizations as artificial intelligence becomes more deeply embedded into how work gets done. In my conversations with leaders, on
digital-culture.dwp_take: The article argues that employee resistance to AI isn't about the technology itself but about fear of job loss and organizational upheaval. This matters to digital workplace pros because it reframes the real problem: we've been focusing on adoption metrics when we should be addressing psychological safety and clarity about roles in an AI-augmented future. Here's the thing though—telling scared people "you're not actually resisting AI, you're just afraid" doesn't make them less scared, it just makes them feel gaslit by management.

digital-culture.title: I’ve been an entrepreneur and a stay-at-home mom, and recently became an empty nester. Here’s how I figured out what’s next
digital-culture.excerpt: Being a mother is a job that most of us do for at least 18 years straight. And it’s a 24/7 role that doesn’t let us take off nights and weekends. Then, provided that we‘ve done it properly, one day we
digital-culture.dwp_take: A woman who's spent 18 years as a stay-at-home parent is navigating the identity crisis that comes when her kids leave home and she needs to figure out what's next professionally. This matters because we're finally acknowledging that career transitions aren't just about job hops, they're about life stage shifts that affect how people think about work, skills, and belonging. After three decades watching people try to "rebrand themselves," I can tell you the real insight here is simple: nobody actually leaves the workforce, they just stop getting paid for their most important work, which is kind of messed up when you think about it.

digital-culture.title: The new rules of work: Multigenerational workplaces in the Gen Z era
digital-culture.excerpt: Four generations are now sharing the same workplace: baby boomers, Gen X, millennials, and Gen Z. Each generation brings different expectations around leadership, communication, flexibility, and AI im
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company reports that four generations now work side by side, each with wildly different expectations about leadership, flexibility, communication, and how to use AI. This matters because your digital workplace strategy can't be a one-size-fits-all anymore, and frankly, your managers need real guidance instead of just hoping everyone gets along. Here's the thing: after thirty years I've learned that every generation thinks the previous one is confused and the next one is lazy, so maybe the real strategy is just building tools flexible enough that nobody has to change their mind about anyone else.

digital-culture.title: As employer burnout costs soar, EY gets at the heart of worker well-being with Vitality Index
digital-culture.excerpt: The tool is designed to help employers measure and boost workforce well-being.
digital-culture.dwp_take: EY launched the Vitality Index, a measurement tool aimed at helping employers track and improve employee well-being as burnout costs keep climbing. For digital workplace leaders, this matters because well-being metrics are becoming as critical as productivity metrics, and you need actual data to justify investments in the tools and policies that combat burnout. Here's the thing though: measuring vitality is great, but only if companies actually act on what they learn instead of just adding another dashboard to ignore.

industry-news.title: Southeast Asia Scam Compounds Turn AI Into a Cybersecurity Threat
industry-news.excerpt: Scam compounds across Southeast Asia are using AI, malware, and automation to scale fraud, forcing APAC security teams to rethink phishing, identity, and mobile-risk controls. The post Southeast Asia
industry-news.dwp_take: Criminal operations in Southeast Asia are weaponizing AI and automation to run sophisticated fraud at scale, which is forcing security teams across the Asia-Pacific region to completely overhaul how they defend against phishing, identity theft, and mobile attacks. This matters because your remote workforce is now dealing with AI-generated scams that are faster, more convincing, and harder to spot than anything your training covered five years ago. The real kicker is that criminals figured out how to make AI work for them before most companies figured out how to make it work for their own security teams.

After years of promising the transition was "just around the corner," Apple is finally pulling the plug, which means some poor workplace tech manager is about to have a very uncomfortable conversation with their CFO about refresh budgets.

industry-news.title: New GitHub Zero-Day Exposed Developer Tokens to Attackers

industry-news.dwp_take: GitHub discovered a zero-day vulnerability in github.dev that allowed attackers to steal OAuth tokens through a single click, potentially exposing private repositories and developer codebases. Here's the thing: we've known for years that token security is the weakest link in developer workflows, yet we keep acting surprised when someone finds a clever way to steal them.

industry-news.dwp_take: Gartner's latest research says organizations need to stop acting like cybersecurity is about keeping the bad guys out and start accepting that they're already in, focusing instead on bouncing back fast when things go sideways. After thirty years in this space, I'll say it plainly: prevention was always a nice idea, but resilience is what actually keeps the lights on when reality crashes the party.
